# Scenario

An ecologist studying a rocky shore at Phillip Island, in southeastern Australia, was interested in how
clumps of intertidal mussels are maintained [@Quinn-1988-137]. In particular, he wanted to know how densities of adult
mussels affected recruitment of young individuals from the plankton. As with most marine invertebrates,
recruitment is highly patchy in time, so he expected to find seasonal variation, and the interaction
between season and density - whether effects of adult mussel density vary across seasons - was the aspect
of most interest.

The data were collected from four seasons, and with two densities of adult mussels. The experiment
consisted of clumps of adult mussels attached to the rocks. These clumps were then brought back to the
laboratory, and the number of baby mussels recorded. There were 3-6 replicate clumps for each density
and season combination.

SEASON   DENSITY   RECRUITS   SQRTRECRUITS   GROUP
-------- --------- ---------- -------------- ------------
Spring   Low       15         3.87           SpringLow
..       ..        ..         ..             ..
Spring   High      11         3.32           SpringHigh
..       ..        ..         ..             ..
Summer   Low       21         4.58           SummerLow
..       ..        ..         ..             ..
Summer   High      34         5.83           SummerHigh
..       ..        ..         ..             ..
Autumn   Low       14         3.74           AutumnLow
..       ..        ..         ..             ..

: Format of the quinn.csv data file {#tbl-quinn .table-condensed}

------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**SEASON**         Categorical listing of Season in which mussel clumps were collected ­ independent variable
**DENSITY**        Categorical listing of the density of mussels within mussel clump ­ independent variable
**RECRUITS**       The number of mussel recruits ­ response variable
**SQRTRECRUITS**   Square root transformation of RECRUITS - needed to meet the test assumptions
**GROUPS**         Categorical listing of Season/Density combinations - used for checking ANOVA assumptions
------------------ --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

: Description of the variables in the quinn data file {#tbl-quinn1 .table-condensed}

![Mussel](../resources/mussels.jpg){#fig-mussel height="300"}

# Read in the data

```{r}
quinn <- read_csv("../data/quinn.csv", trim_ws = TRUE)
```

# Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| label: label
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn |> ggplot(aes(y = RECRUITS, x = SEASON, fill = DENSITY)) +
  geom_boxplot() 

#appears to be a relationship between mean and variance (lower mean = lower variance)

#don't ever do sqrt transformation, it's sooo hard to back transform

#need to check if it's zero inflated --> there are some in winter
```

Model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{NB}(\lambda_i, \theta)\\
ln(\mu_i) &= \beta_0 + \sum_{j=1}^nT_{[i],j}.\beta_j\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(2.4, 0.2)\\
\beta_{[1,2,3]} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 2.5)\\
\end{align}
$$

where $\beta_{0}$ is the y-intercept (mean of the first group),
$\beta_{[1,2,3]}$ are the vector of effects parameters (contrasting
each group mean to that of the first group and $T{[i],j}$ represents a
$i$ by $j$ model matrix is a model matrix representing the season,
density and their interaction on mussel recruitment.

OR alternatively, we could write this as

Model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{NB}(\lambda_i, \theta)\\
ln(\mu_i) &= \boldsymbol{\beta} \bf{X_i}\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(2.4, 0.2)\\
\beta_{[1,2,3]} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 2.5)\\
\end{align}
$$

where $\beta_{0}$ is the y-intercept (mean of the first group),
$\beta_{[1,2,3]}$ are the vector of effects parameters (contrasting
each group mean to that of the first group and $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is
a vector of effects parameters (including the intercept) and
$\bf{X_i}$ is a model matrix representing the intercept and treatment
contrasts for the effects of density and season on mussel recruitment.


```{r dataprep, results='markdown', eval=TRUE}
## A recent bug has infiltrated emmeans such that SEASON seems
## to be some sort of keyword.  So in order to prevent downstream issues
## when declaring season as a factor, we will also alter its name...
quinn <- quinn |>
  mutate(fSEASON = factor(SEASON,
                         levels = c("Spring", "Summer", "Autumn", "Winter")),
                         DENSITY = factor(DENSITY))
```

# Fit the model
```{r}
#| label: define model formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_form <- bf(RECRUITS ~ fSEASON*DENSITY, family = poisson(link = 'log'))
```

```{r}
#| label: priors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(quinn_form, data = quinn)

#adding +1 so that we don't have to deal with 0s. Thats also why we use both mean and median and so on
quinn |> 
  group_by(fSEASON, DENSITY) |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(log(RECRUITS+1)),
            median = median(log(RECRUITS+1)),
            SD = sd(log(RECRUITS+1)),
            MAD = mad(log(RECRUITS+1))) 


priors <- prior(normal(2.4,0.8), class = 'Intercept') +
  prior(normal(0,1.3), class = 'b')
#doesn't need to be exact number, just whatever is close to the mean/median and SD/MAD
```

# MCMC sampling diagnostics
```{r}
#| label: prior only model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

#stan uses no u turn sampler (NUTS)
quinn_brm2 <- brm(quinn_form,
                 data=quinn,
                 prior=priors,
                 sample_prior="only",
                 iter=5000,
                 chains=3, cores=3, #one core per chain
                 warmup=1000,
                 thin=5,
                 backend="cmdstanr",
                 refresh=0, 
                 seed = 1)

```
```{r}
#| label: plot model quinn_brm2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brm2 |> 
  conditional_effects('fSEASON:DENSITY') |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

```

```{r}
#| label: sample from prior and data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

quinn_brm3 <- update(quinn_brm2, sample_prior = 'yes', refresh = 0, seed = 1)

```

```{r}
#| label: plot model quinn_brm3
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brm3 |> 
  conditional_effects('fSEASON:DENSITY') |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#now model looks much more refined
#and looks like data is driving the trend, not priors which is what we want
```
```{r}
#| label: examine all priors and posteriors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brm3 |> 
  SUYR_prior_and_posterior()
```

# Model validation
```{r}
#| label: model diagnostics
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brm3$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

quinn_brm3$fit |> stan_ac()

quinn_brm3$fit |> stan_rhat()

quinn_brm3$fit |> stan_ess()
```
```{r}
#| label: posterior probs density overlay
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brm3 |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)

#dark line is actual distribution of our data
#our model reconstructs the data okayyy
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(quinn_brm3, integerResponse = TRUE)
testUniformity(quinn.resids)
plotResiduals(quinn.resids, quantreg = TRUE)
testDispersion(quinn.resids)

#to the right = overdispersion
#to the left = underdispersed

#ours is overdispered, more variability than our model expected

#when you look at species that aggregate, you get things the model can't account for --> you could account for this with an observation level random effect
#so we use a negative binomial
```

# Explore negative binomial model
## because we only have a few 0s

```{r}
#| label: formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_form <- bf(RECRUITS ~ fSEASON*DENSITY, family = negbinomial(link = 'log'))
```

```{r}
#| label: add extra prior
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#negbinomial has 2 parameters so we need 2 priors now
get_prior(quinn_form, data = quinn)

#visualize this
standist::visualize("inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3)")

#compare with this standard prior for overdispersion
standist::visualize("inv_gamma(0.4, 0.3)", "gamma(0.01, 0.01")
#0.01, 0.01 is a wider prior than the other one
#but our dispersion was about 2.5 so either of these priors would appropriately encompass this

#add this new prior to our OG priors
priors <- priors + prior(inv_gamma(0.4,0.3), class = "shape")
```

```{r}
#| label: prior only model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

priors <- prior(normal(2.4,0.8), class = 'Intercept') +
  prior(normal(0,1.3), class = 'b') + 
  prior(gamma(0.01,0.01), class = "shape")
  

#stan uses no u turn sampler (NUTS)
quinn_brmsNB <- brm(quinn_form,
                 data=quinn,
                 prior=priors,
                 iter=5000,
                 chains=3, cores=3, #one core per chain
                 warmup=1000,
                 thin=5,
                 backend="cmdstanr",
                 refresh=0, 
                 seed = 1)

```

```{r}
#| label: model diagnostics
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn_brmsNB$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

quinn_brmsNB$fit |> stan_ac()

quinn_brmsNB$fit |> stan_rhat()

quinn_brmsNB$fit |> stan_ess()
```
```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

quinn.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(quinn_brmsNB, integerResponse = TRUE)
testUniformity(quinn.resids)
plotResiduals(quinn.resids, quantreg = TRUE)
testDispersion(quinn.resids)

#instead of AIC, we use looic
#it only means something if we compare it to another model
loo(quinn_brmsNB) #298
loo(quinn_brm3) #338
#so negative binomial is better

#can also do
loo_compare(loo(quinn_brmsNB), loo(quinn_brm3)) #Neg binomial is 20x better than brm3 or 40x better on AIC scale
```
